questions.q: A C array is described as an *ordered* collection of elements. What does "ordered" mean here?
choices: Each element is at a specific position (position 0, position 1, and so on)
The values are always kept sorted in ascending order
Elements are stored in the order they were most recently accessed
The values must be inserted from smallest to largest
questions.explain: Ordered means each element has a specific position in the collection. It does not mean the values are sorted.

questions.q: True or false: A single C array can hold a mix of `int` and `char` values.
questions.explain: Every element of a C array has the same type, which you give when you declare the array.

questions.q: Which of the following must you specify when you declare a statically declared array variable in C?
choices: The type of each element
The total capacity (maximum number of elements)
The initial value of every element
The number of elements currently in use
questions.explain: A declaration like `int arr[10];` gives the element type (int) and the capacity (10). The program has to track how many elements are in use itself, for example with a separate size variable.

questions.q: How are the elements of a C array laid out in the program's memory?
choices: In consecutive memory locations, so each element comes immediately after the previous one
At scattered locations, linked together by pointers
In reverse order, with the last element at the lowest address
Wherever the compiler finds free space, in no defined order
questions.explain: C defines the array layout: elements are stored in consecutive locations. For example, the third position comes right after the second and right before the fourth.

questions.q: True or false: Like Python lists, C arrays have built-in operations such as `len`, `append`, and `insert`.
questions.explain: C arrays only provide low-level storage. The programmer has to implement higher-level features, such as keeping track of the number of elements.

questions.q: Given the declaration `int arr[25];`, what is the largest valid index into `arr`?
questions.explain: Valid indices run from 0 to capacity minus 1, so here they are 0 through 24.

choices: It compiles, and its runtime behavior is undefined
The compiler reports an error and refuses to compile it
The program raises an IndexError at runtime
The array automatically grows to hold 11 elements
questions.explain: 10 is not a valid index for an array of capacity 10. The compiler accepts the code and nothing checks bounds at runtime, so the behavior is undefined.

questions.q: A C program writes to an index past the end of an array. Which of the following could happen?
choices: The program crashes
Another variable's value changes
Nothing visibly changes in the program's behavior
The compiler refuses to compile the program
questions.explain: The behavior is undefined. The program might crash, corrupt another variable, or seem to work, and the result can differ from run to run. The compiler still compiles the code.

questions.q: True or false: C checks array bounds at runtime, so an invalid index always stops the program with an error.
questions.explain: C does no bounds checking, either at compile time or at runtime. It is up to the programmer to use only valid indices.
The loop sets `arr[i] = i * 2` for i = 0 to 4, so `arr[4]` is 4 * 2 = 8. The line `arr[5] = 100` sets the next element.

questions.q: How can you access the elements of a C array?
choices: Only by indexing (e.g., `arr[i]`)
By indexing and by slicing (e.g., `arr[2:5]`)
By indexing, including negative indices that count from the end
Only through built-in iterator functions
questions.explain: Python has several ways to access list elements, but C supports only indexing.

questions.q: When you pass an array as an argument to a C function, what does the array parameter receive?
choices: A copy of the array's base address
A separate copy of every element in the array
The number of elements in the array
Only the value of the element at index 0
questions.explain: C passes arguments by value, and the value of an array name is its base address. The parameter gets a copy of that address, so it refers to the same storage as the argument.

questions.q: In C, the name of an array variable (for example, `arr`) is equivalent to which of the following?
choices: The memory location of its 0th element (its base address)
The value stored in its 0th element
The number of elements in the array
A copy of all of the array's elements
questions.explain: An array's name is equivalent to its base address, which is the memory location of element 0.
Parameter `a` holds the base address of `nums`, so both names refer to the same storage. Setting `a[1] = 50` changes `nums[1]`, and the change remains after the function returns.

questions.q: In the same program (`change` sets `a[1] = 50` and `size = 0`, then `main` prints `nums[1]` and `n`), what is the value of `n` when the `printf` runs?
questions.explain: `size` is a copy of `n`. Setting `size = 0` changes only the parameter, so `n` stays 4.

questions.q: Why do C functions that take an array parameter almost always take a separate size parameter too?
choices: You can't get an array's size or capacity from the array variable alone
C requires every function to have at least two parameters
The size parameter tells the compiler how much memory to copy
Without it, the function can't modify the array's elements
questions.explain: The array parameter is just the base address. It carries no size or capacity information, so the caller passes the size separately.

questions.q: True or false: A function declared as `void print_array(int arr[], int size)` can be called with an `int` array of any capacity.
questions.explain: The `[]` without a capacity means the parameter is an array of int of any capacity.
The first loop sets more[0..4] to 0, 1, 4, 9, 16. Then more[5] = more[4] + more[3] = 16 + 9 = 25.

questions.q: What is the name of the special character `'\0'` that marks the end of a C string?
questions.explain: C strings must end with the null character `'\0'`. Strings that end this way are called null-terminated.

questions.q: What is the minimum number of `char` elements an array needs to store the string `"hello"`?
questions.explain: The array needs 5 elements for the characters h, e, l, l, o and 1 more for the terminating `'\0'`.

questions.q: True or false: Every character array in C is a C string.
questions.explain: Every C string is a character array, but not every character array is used as a string.

questions.q: Why must C strings end with a null character?
choices: The array holding a string may be bigger than the string, so you can't use the array's size as the string's length
The null character tells the compiler to allocate more memory for the string
C requires every array, of any type, to end with a null value
The null character makes the string read-only
questions.explain: Arrays are often declared larger than the data they hold. The `'\0'` marks where the string actually ends.

questions.q: Which `printf` format placeholder prints a string?
questions.explain: `%s` prints the characters of the array argument up to the `'\0'`.

questions.q: True or false: Like Python, C has a built-in string type that is separate from arrays.
questions.explain: C has no string type. Strings are arrays of `char` values ending with `'\0'`.

questions.q: When `printf` prints a string with `%s`, how does it know where to stop?
choices: It stops when it reaches the `'\0'` character
It always prints the full capacity of the array
It stops at the first space character
It reads a hidden length field stored with the array
questions.explain: `printf` prints characters until it reaches the null character.

questions.q: Which header file must a program include to use C string library functions such as `strlen` and `strcpy`?
questions.explain: The string library functions are declared in `string.h`.
`strlen` counts the characters before the null character. The `'\0'` is not counted, and neither is the array's capacity, so the result is 3.

questions.q: True or false: The value returned by `strlen` includes the string's terminating null character.
questions.explain: The terminating `'\0'` is not part of the string's length. For example, `strlen` of "hi" is 2.

questions.q: In the call `strcpy(dest, src)`, what happens?
choices: Characters are copied from `src` into `dest`, one at a time, until the null character in `src` is reached
Characters are copied from `dest` into `src` until `dest`'s null character is reached
`dest` is made to refer to the same storage as `src`
`src` is appended to the end of the string already in `dest`
questions.explain: The first parameter is the destination and the second is the source. `strcpy` copies characters from the source until it reaches the source's `'\0'`.

questions.q: Which of these situations can cause undefined behavior when calling `strcpy(dest, src)`?
choices: `dest` is too small to hold the string in `src`
`src` has no terminating `'\0'` character
`dest` has much more capacity than `src` needs
`src` is a string literal such as `"hello"`
questions.explain: If the destination is too small, `strcpy` writes past its end. If the source is missing its `'\0'`, `strcpy` keeps reading past the end of the source array. A large destination and a literal source are both fine.

questions.q: Why is `strcpy` considered a security risk?
choices: It assumes the destination is large enough for the whole source string, which may not be true (for example, with user input)
It sends the copied string over the network
It removes the null character from the destination string
It always leaks the memory of the source string
questions.explain: `strcpy` does not check the destination's capacity. If the source is longer than expected, as can happen with user input, the copy writes past the end of the destination.
